mainTopic: The end of the חצי עבד וחצי בן חורין debate, and which kind of חרש is exempt from ראייה and from שמחה.
overview: This amud finishes the debate about a person who is half slave and half free. בית שמאי point out that he cannot marry anyone, even though the world was created to be filled with people. So the master is forced to free him, and the slave writes a document owing his master half his value. בית הלל agree to this. Then the גמרא goes back to our משנה's words 'except for a חרש, שוטה and קטן.' Because the חרש is listed with people who lack understanding, he must be someone who neither hears nor speaks. A person who only cannot hear, or only cannot speak, counts as fully capable. A ברייתא seems to say such a person is exempt, so רבינא (or רבא) explains that our משנה is missing words. Such a person is exempt from ראייה but still obligated in שמחה. A full חרש, a שוטה and a קטן are exempt from both. A ברייתא supporting this begins at the end of the amud and finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: בית שמאי: You helped the master but not the half-slave
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי argue against בית הלל's arrangement: it takes care of the master but leaves the half-slave stuck, because he cannot marry anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: You fixed things for his master, but you did not fix things for him. He cannot marry a maidservant, and he cannot marry a free woman.
steps.whatsHappening: בית שמאי attack בית הלל's plan of letting the half-slave work one day for himself and one day for his master. They point out that he has no one he can marry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because half of him is free, he may not marry a שפחה. Because half of him is still a slave, he may not marry a בת חורין. So בית הלל's plan protects the master's money but leaves the person himself trapped.

keyTerms.meaning: You have fixed or arranged things
His master
A non-Jewish maidservant
A free woman

steps.confusionAlert: Who is talking? This is still בית שמאי speaking, continuing the quoted משנה about the half-slave. It is not the גמרא's own question.

phrases.english: You have fixed things for his master,
phrases.notes: בית שמאי are talking to בית הלל about someone who is half slave and half free.

phrases.english: but for himself you have not fixed things.
To marry a maidservant he cannot,
and a free woman he cannot.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּקַּנְתֶּם אֶת רַבּוֹ, וְאֶת עַצְמוֹ לֹא תִּקַּנְתֶּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues בית שמאי's response to בית הלל's ruling about the half-slave, which began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: בית הלל's arrangement of splitting the half-slave's days between himself and his master.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The arrangement leaves him with no permitted marriage partner, so it does not really solve his situation.

steps.title: He cannot just stay unmarried, because the world was made to be filled
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי block the idea that he could simply never marry, quoting a פסוק that the world was created to be lived in.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should he just do nothing and not marry? But the world was created only for having children, as it says: 'He did not create it to be empty; He formed it to be lived in.'
steps.whatsHappening: בית שמאי answer an obvious reply before anyone can make it: 'So let him stay single.' They say that is not acceptable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיהו shows that filling the world with people is the purpose of creation. So leaving a person with no way to have children is a real problem, not a small one. This makes the challenge from step 1 even stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him stay idle, meaning not marry at all
Being fruitful and multiplying, having children
Emptiness, waste

phrases.english: Should he just stay idle?
phrases.notes: This is a suggestion that he simply never marry, which בית שמאי are about to reject.

phrases.english: But wasn't the world created
only for being fruitful and multiplying,
as it says: 'He did not create it to be empty;
He formed it to be lived in.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לִיבְטֵּיל — וַהֲלֹא לֹא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם אֶלָּא לִפְרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Blocks a possible escape from the problem raised in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense that the half-slave could simply stay unmarried.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Having children is the purpose of creation, so leaving him unmarried is not an acceptable outcome.

steps.title: The solution: force the master to free him
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי's ruling: because of תיקון העולם, the master is forced to free him, and the slave writes a debt document for half his value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, for the betterment of the world, we force his master to make him a free man, and the slave writes him a document owing half his value.
steps.whatsHappening: Having shown the problem, בית שמאי now give their own solution. The master must set the slave completely free, and he is paid back for the half he still owned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fixes both sides. The slave becomes fully free and can marry a Jewish woman. The master does not lose money, because the slave owes him half his value in writing.

keyTerms.meaning: The betterment of the world, a rule set up for society's good
We force
A free man
A written document, here a debt document
His value or price

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a clear example of a ruling made מפני תיקון העולם, where the court forces an owner's hand for the good of society.

phrases.english: Rather, for the betterment of the world,
we force his master
and he makes him a free man,
and he writes him a document
phrases.notes: Here the slave is the one writing, giving his master a written promise to pay.

phrases.english: for half his value.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִפְּנֵי תִּיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם, כּוֹפִין אֶת רַבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives בית שמאי's own ruling after showing the problem with בית הלל's approach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The master is forced to free the half-slave, who then owes the master half his value through a written document.

steps.title: בית הלל change their ruling
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל take back their view and rule like בית שמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And בית הלל went back and ruled like בית שמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The debate ends: בית הלל agree with בית שמאי that the half-slave must be set free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is one of the rare cases where בית הלל accept בית שמאי's view. So the final הלכה follows בית שמאי here, and a half-slave is fully freed.

keyTerms.meaning: And they took back their view
To rule, to teach the הלכה

steps.whatToRemember: A half-slave cannot marry anyone, so because of תיקון העולם his master is forced to free him in return for a debt of half his value. בית הלל agreed to this.

phrases.english: And Beit Hillel went back to rule
like the words of Beit Shammai.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזְרוּ בֵּית הִלֵּל לְהוֹרוֹת כְּדִבְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the half-slave discussion by recording that בית הלל agreed with בית שמאי.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows בית שמאי: the half-slave is freed by force, and he owes his master half his value.

steps.title: The חרש in our משנה lacks understanding, like the others listed with him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's list 'חרש, שוטה וקטן.' Since the חרש is listed with people who lack understanding, he too must be someone who lacks understanding.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Except for a חרש, a שוטה and a קטן.' It lists the חרש together with the שוטה and קטן. Just as they lack understanding, so too this חרש lacks understanding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a phrase in our משנה and learns something from the order of the list. Because the חרש is grouped with the שוטה and קטן, he must be like them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שוטה and קטן are exempt because they lack דעת, full understanding. Putting the חרש next to them shows that the חרש here is also someone without full understanding, not just someone with a hearing problem. This sets up the next step, which defines exactly who that is.

keyTerms.meaning: Usually a deaf-mute; here, who exactly counts is being defined
A mentally incompetent person
A minor
Similar to, in the same category as
A person of sound mind and understanding

phrases.english: Except for a deaf-mute, an insane person, and a minor, etc.
It lists the deaf-mute alongside the insane person and the minor:
Just as an insane person and a minor
are not people of sound mind,

phrases.aramaic: אַף חֵרֵשׁ — דְּלָאו בַּר דֵּעָה הוּא.
phrases.english: so too the deaf-mute is one who is not of sound mind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to another phrase of the משנה after the half-slave discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חרש exempted in the משנה is one who, like the שוטה and קטן, lacks full understanding.

steps.title: The standard definition: one who neither hears nor speaks
steps.stepSummary: This matches a משנה in תרומות: the חרש the חכמים speak of everywhere is one who neither hears nor speaks. So someone who can only hear or only speak is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us what we learned in a משנה: the חרש the חכמים talk about everywhere is one who does not hear and does not speak. So one who speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects step 5 to a well-known משנה that defines the חרש. From that definition, it concludes who is still obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only a person who both cannot hear and cannot speak counts as a חרש without understanding. A person missing only one of these is considered fully capable, so he is obligated. Step 12 will narrow this: he is exempt from ראייה but obligated in שמחה.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us
As we learned in a משנה
Everywhere, in every place in the תורה שבעל פה
Obligated

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think every deaf person is exempt. In הלכה, the 'חרש' is specifically someone who can neither hear nor speak. A person who can do one of the two is obligated.

phrases.english: And it teaches us what we learned in a Mishnah:
phrases.notes: The משנה quoted here is from מסכת תרומות.

phrases.english: The deaf-mute that the Sages spoke of everywhere
is one who does not hear and does not speak.
So one who speaks but does not hear,
or hears but does not speak, is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses a known משנה to define exactly which חרש step 5 is talking about.
steps.raayaObject: That the חרש exempted is only one who both cannot hear and cannot speak.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in תרומות: 'חרש שדיברו חכמים בכל מקום שאינו שומע ואינו מדבר.'

steps.title: A ברייתא already says this: deaf or mute alone counts as fully capable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that a ברייתא already teaches this: one who speaks but can't hear is a 'חרש,' one who hears but can't speak is an 'אילם,' and both are treated as fully capable in all matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: We already learned this, as the Rabbis taught: one who speaks but does not hear is called a חרש; one who hears but does not speak is called an אילם. Both are like fully capable people in everything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that a ברייתא already says what step 6 concluded. This backs up the idea that a person missing only hearing or only speech is fully capable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives names to the partial cases: speaks but can't hear is a 'חרש,' hears but can't speak is an 'אילם.' It says both count as פקחין, fully capable people. This matches the conclusion that they are obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: We have already learned this
A mute person, who hears but cannot speak
Fully capable people, of sound mind and senses

steps.whatToRemember: The חרש who is exempt from all מצוות is only one who neither hears nor speaks. Someone who only cannot hear, or only cannot speak, counts as a פקח. Step 12 shows he is still exempt from ראייה but obligated in שמחה.

phrases.english: We already learned this, as the Rabbis taught:
One who speaks but does not hear, this is a deaf person,
one who hears but does not speak, this is a mute,
this one and that one are like fully capable people
in all their matters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that already states the conclusion reached in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That someone who only cannot hear, or only cannot speak, has the full status of a capable person.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: 'זה וזה הרי הן כפקחין לכל דבריהם.'

steps.title: Where do the names 'deaf' and 'mute' come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that חרש means someone who can't hear, and אילם means someone who can't speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know that a person who speaks but can't hear is called a חרש, and a person who hears but can't speak is called an אילם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the two names used in the ברייתא it just quoted. It is setting up an answer from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in Step 7 gave each type of person his own name. The גמרא wants to know what tells us that חרש is about hearing and אילם is about speaking, and not the other way around.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know?
A mute person, who hears but cannot speak

phrases.english: And from where do we know that one who speaks but does not hear
is the one called a deaf person,
and one who hears but does not speak is the one called a mute?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִמַּאי דִּמְדַבֵּר וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵעַ זֶהוּ חֵרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the names used in the ברייתא of Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that חרש means 'can't hear' and אילם means 'can't speak'.

steps.title: A פסוק in תהלים links each name to its disability
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק pairs חרש with not hearing and אילם with not opening the mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'I am like a חרש who does not hear, and like an אילם who does not open his mouth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק that matches each word to its problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, חרש goes together with 'I do not hear' and אילם goes together with 'does not open his mouth.' So the meanings are fixed: חרש is about hearing and אילם is about speech.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (a פסוק is being quoted)

phrases.english: As it is written: “But I am like a deaf man, I do not hear;
and like a mute who does not open his mouth.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק links חרש to not hearing and אילם to not speaking.

steps.title: A second answer from an everyday saying
steps.stepSummary: The word אילם is explained by the common phrase 'his speech has been taken.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say it comes from how people talk: 'his speech has been taken away.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, separate answer to the same question, this time from everyday Aramaic speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of a פסוק, the word אילם itself is tied to a known phrase about losing speech. This also shows that אילם describes someone who can't speak.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say instead (introduces a second answer)
His speech has been taken away

phrases.english: And if you wish, say instead: as people commonly say:
“His speech has been taken away.”
phrases.notes: The word אילם is read as built from the opening letters of this phrase, so it means someone whose speech is gone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to Step 8, as an alternative to the פסוק in Step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word אילם comes from the phrase 'his speech has been taken.'

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to clash with our משנה: obligated or exempt?
steps.stepSummary: One source says a person who only speaks or only hears is obligated. Another ברייתא says he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said that someone who speaks but can't hear, or hears but can't speak, is obligated. But a ברייתא teaches that such people are exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the ruling from Steps 6–7 against a different ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 6–7 said a partly deaf or partly mute person is treated as fully capable, so he is obligated. Now a ברייתא calls the very same people פטור. Both cannot be true as they stand, so the גמרא needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Obligated
Exempt

phrases.english: One who speaks but does not hear,
phrases.notes: This repeats the ruling we just saw in Steps 6 and 7.

phrases.english: or one who hears but does not speak, is obligated.
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא: one who speaks but does not hear,
or one who hears but does not speak, is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: מְדַבֵּר וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵעַ, שׁוֹמֵעַ וְאֵינוֹ מְדַבֵּר — פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of Steps 6–7 with a ברייתא that seems to disagree.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that one who only speaks or only hears is obligated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא calls the same people exempt, which is a direct contradiction.

steps.title: Exempt from ראייה, but obligated in שמחה
steps.stepSummary: רבינא (or רבא) says the text is missing words. Partly deaf or mute people are exempt only from ראייה and still obligated in שמחה. A full חרש, a שוטה, and a קטן are exempt even from שמחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing, and this is what the text means: everyone is obligated in ראייה and שמחה, except a חרש who speaks but can't hear and one who hears but can't speak. They are exempt from ראייה, but they are still obligated in שמחה. But one who can neither hear nor speak, a שוטה, and a קטן are exempt even from שמחה, because they are exempt from all the מצוות in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא (or רבא) resolves the contradiction by saying our משנה is missing words. He fills them in so that the partly deaf or partly mute person is exempt only from ראייה but obligated in שמחה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sources are talking about different מצוות. 'Exempt' means exempt from ראייה, and 'obligated' fits שמחה and the other מצוות. Only someone who lacks understanding, a full חרש, a שוטה, or a קטן, is exempt from everything, including שמחה.

keyTerms.meaning: Words are missing from the text
And this is what it teaches
The מצוה to appear at the בית המקדש on the רגל
The מצוה to rejoice on the רגל

steps.whatToRemember: A person who only speaks or only hears is exempt from ראייה but obligated in שמחה. A full חרש, a שוטה, and a קטן are exempt from both, because they are exempt from all מצוות.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'exempt' ruling is not saying this person falls outside the מצוות in general. He is exempt from ראייה only; he is still obligated in שמחה and the other מצוות.

phrases.english: Ravina said, and some say it was Rava:
Words are missing, and this is what it teaches:
phrases.notes: He means our משנה is missing words. What follows is how it should read in full.

phrases.english: Everyone is obligated in appearing and in rejoicing,
except a deaf person who speaks but does not hear,
or one who hears but does not speak,
who is exempt from appearing.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפָּטוּר מִן הָרְאִיָּיה,
phrases.english: And even though he is exempt from appearing,
he is obligated in rejoicing.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶת שֶׁאֵינוֹ לֹא שׁוֹמֵעַ וְלֹא מְדַבֵּר,
phrases.english: But one who neither hears nor speaks,
and a mentally incompetent person and a minor —
is exempt even from rejoicing,

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וּפְטוּרִים מִכׇּל מִצְוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה.
phrases.english: since they are exempt from all the מצוות stated in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Fills in missing words in our משנה, so that 'exempt' (the ברייתא) refers to ראייה and 'obligated' refers to שמחה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה (as read with the משנה in תרומות) implies a partly deaf or partly mute person is obligated, while a ברייתא says he is exempt, so the sources seem to disagree.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is exempt from ראייה only, and obligated in שמחה. Only those lacking understanding are exempt from everything.

steps.title: A ברייתא that teaches this same idea
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that says just what רבינא proposed: those who only speak or only hear are exempt from ראייה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: everyone is obligated in ראייה and שמחה, except a חרש who speaks but can't hear and one who hears but can't speak. They are exempt from ראייה. And even though they are exempt from ראייה —
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רבינא's answer. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא's version was his own reconstruction of the missing words. Here an actual ברייתא is found that says the same thing, which backs up his answer.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא also teaches this (a support)

phrases.english: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא:
Everyone is obligated in appearing and in rejoicing,
except a deaf person who speaks but does not hear,
or one who hears but does not speak,
as they are exempt from appearing.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפָּטוּר מִן הָרְאִיָּיה —
phrases.english: And even though he is exempt from appearing —
phrases.notes: The sentence breaks off here and finishes on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 12 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבינא's answer that a partly deaf or partly mute person is exempt only from ראייה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says the same thing.
